opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at that time it felt almost like an obvious choice. Around 2017, 2018, FAIR was kind of the center of gravity for computer vision. You had people like Kaiming, Ross Girshick, Piotr Dollár, and many others all in one place. These were people whose papers I had read line by line as a PhD student, and suddenly you could just walk over to their desk and argue about an idea.

I also had interned there before, so I knew the culture firsthand. What struck me most was how open it was. It was truly research-driven. Nobody told you, "you need to ship this feature next quarter." The expectation was to work on problems you believed were important, publish openly, release code, and let the community build on it. For someone who cared about fundamental questions, like how we should design architectures and how visual representations should be learned, that freedom was extremely rare, even compared with many academic labs.

Another thing was the taste. At FAIR, especially in the vision group, there was a very strong sense of what good research looks like: simple, clean, and something that actually works and that people will use. Working with Kaiming on things like ResNeXt really shaped me. You learn to strip away unnecessary complexity and find the one idea that matters. That kind of training is hard to get anywhere else.

And of course there were the resources. Compute matters in vision, and FAIR had the infrastructure to try ideas at scale without fighting for GPUs every day. So it was a combination of people, culture, freedom, and resources. At that moment I couldn't think of a better place to grow as a researcher.

r001.rationale: He calls FAIR the center of gravity for computer vision and cites leading researchers gathered there as a reason it was an obvious choice.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I was finishing my PhD at UC San Diego around 2017, FAIR felt like the center of gravity for computer vision. Kaiming He was there, Ross Girshick was there, Piotr Dollár, and I had already been collaborating with Kaiming on ResNeXt during my internship, so I had seen from the inside how that group worked. It wasn't just that the people were strong individually. It was that the whole culture was built around doing fundamental, open research and then actually publishing it, releasing the code, and letting the community build on it. Detectron came out of that environment. That mattered a lot to me, because I never wanted to do work that disappeared into a product and nobody could reproduce.

The other thing was compute and freedom at the same time. In academia you have freedom but you're always fighting for GPUs. In a lot of industry labs you have compute but somebody is telling you what to work on every quarter. FAIR at that moment had both. Nobody told me what to do. You just sat next to people you really respected, argued about ideas on the whiteboard, and had enough resources to test them seriously. For a young researcher who cared about architectures and representation learning, that combination was hard to find anywhere else. So it wasn't really a hard decision. It was more like, where else would I go?

r001.rationale: He says FAIR felt like the center of gravity for computer vision and names several leading researchers there as part of why it was the right destination for him.

astra-6.text:
At the time, FAIR felt like a place where I could really focus on fundamental research. You had the resources of a large company, but also a very open, academic research culture. You could pursue longer-term questions, publish your work, and share it with the community.

And for computer vision, the people were a huge part of the attraction. I wanted to be around researchers whose work I admired, to learn from them and exchange ideas. It wasn’t that I had compared every institution and proved FAIR was the best. It was that the combination of people, openness, and freedom to explore felt like the right environment for me.

r001.rationale: The response says Xie was drawn to researchers whose work he admired, but it does not clearly identify a concentration of leading computer-vision researchers as his reason for considering FAIR the best destination.

sol-6.1.text:
At the time, I felt FAIR offered a rare combination: a strong group of people working on computer vision, the resources to pursue ambitious ideas, and the freedom to do fundamental research. You could ask a question because it was scientifically interesting, without needing to connect it immediately to a product.

For me, the people were especially important. I wanted to be somewhere I could learn from colleagues, exchange ideas openly, and develop my own research direction. FAIR seemed like a very good environment for that.

r001.rationale: The response names FAIR’s strong group of people working in computer vision as part of why it seemed like a very good research environment at the time, conveying the criterion’s point about a concentration of strong CV researchers.
